entry.title: Sarah Mcinnes v Le Luxe Design & Construct Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4064
entry.content:
Ms McInnes filed an unfair dismissal application on 20 August 2026, 87 days after her employment was said to have ended on 25 May 2026, outside the 21-day statutory period. The Fair Work Commission was not satisfied there were exceptional circumstances and dismissed the extension application.

Key holding: Under s 394(3) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), the Commission must be satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist before extending time for an unfair dismissal application, regardless of the length of delay.

Regardless of the length of the delay, where an application is lodged outside the statutory time limit, the Commission must be satisfied that there are exceptional circumstances supporting an extension of time.

entry.title: Michiaki Miyazaki v Sydney Omakase Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 3383
entry.content:
Miyazaki v Sydney Omakase Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 3383 concerned an unfair dismissal claim by a Head Chef dismissed for alleged drinking at work. The Fair Work Commission found the employer’s summary dismissal was not consistent with the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code and that the dismissal was harsh, unjust and unreasonable. Compensation was awarded.

Key holding: A dismissal is not consistent with the Summary Dismissal limb of the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code where the employer’s actual reason is a performance concern rather than a belief, held on reasonable grounds at dismissal, that the employee’s conduct was sufficiently serious to justify immediate dismissal.

I do not accept that Mr Best, on behalf of Sydney Omakase, held a belief that Mr Miyazaki's conduct was sufficiently serious to justify immediate dismissal. This is because I find that the reason for dismissal, based on Mr Best's witness statement, was that Mr Miyazaki was unable to confirm that he had the passion to continue as Head Chef.

entry.title: Kacy Brazier v OS MCAP Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4043
entry.content:
This Fair Work Commission decision concerns an order for lost pay following an earlier finding that Kacy Brazier was unfairly dismissed and an order for his reinstatement. The Commission awarded reduced lost pay under s 391 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) because Brazier made no real attempt to find paid work for most of his unemployment and performed unpaid work for his then partner. The total compensation ordered was $98,965.03 gross less tax plus $11,875.80 superannuation.

Key holding: An order to restore lost pay is discretionary and a deliberate failure to mitigate loss may reduce or defeat any award.

It cannot be said that he was unsophisticated or unaware that a deliberate failure to mitigate his loss would affect any award of lost pay at the Commission's discretion.

entry.title: Application by Transport Workers' Union of Australia (179V) [2026] FWC 4051
entry.content:
Deputy President Hampton determined a s.437 protected action ballot order application by the TWU for Cleanaway employees covered by three regional Victorian waste enterprise agreements. The employer objected to scope and ballot questions 5, 9 and 10, including safety-related wording; the Commission rejected the continuing objections and granted the application, with leave to amend some questions. The ballot will be run by Fair Vote Services Pty Ltd and close on 5 November 2026.

Key holding: Under s.443(1) and (3)(d), where a valid s.437 application proposes clear ballot questions, the Commission must make a PABO and has no general discretion to exclude valid questions or amend them merely due to employer objections to wording.

The inference to be drawn from the mandatory nature of s 443(1) is that the order required to be made is one which gives effect to an application validly made under s 437. Thus, in respect of s 443(3)(d), we do not consider that the Commission has a general discretion to determine the questions which will be included in the order, or to simply exclude valid questions, independent of what has been applied for.

entry.title: Roberto Biguzzi v Eco Alliance Pty. Ltd. [2026] FWC 3872
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission dealt with an unfair dismissal application by a former Senior Sales Representative whose role was made redundant after the employer closed its internal sales function. The employer asserted genuine redundancy under s 389, but the Commission found the job was no longer required due operational requirements while the written consultation did not satisfy cl 27.2 of the Miscellaneous Award 2020. The provided extract does not include final orders on the remaining s 387 merits.

Key holding: For a genuine redundancy defence under s 389(1)(b), written consultation must explain the nature of the major change itself, not merely its effects or causes.

It would in my view be insufficient to meet the written notice requirements in clause 27.2 to deal only with the effects of the changes without explaining what the changes actually are. This is consistent with "nature" and "effect" being separately itemised in paragraphs (a) and (b) of clause 27.2.

entry.title: Peter Andrew Staas v Assta Labels Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4050
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission determined an unfair dismissal application by Peter Staas against his family company employer, Assta Labels Pty Ltd, under s.394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). Mr Staas was dismissed after repeatedly refusing to attend an independent medical examination, and the Commission found there was a valid reason and procedural fairness, dismissing the application.

Key holding: A direction to attend an independent medical examination can be lawful and reasonable—and refusal can supply a valid reason for dismissal—where the employee’s health is causally linked to ongoing performance concerns and the employer seeks to assess capacity and possible adjustments.

I am satisfied that the direction to attend an independent medical examination was lawful and reasonable each time a direction was given to Peter in the last four months of his employment. Peter 's refusal to follow this lawful and reasonable direction was a valid reason to dismiss him from his employment with Assta Labels.

entry.title: Mr Muhammad Ahsan Malik v On The Run Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4054
entry.content:
Mr Malik filed an unfair dismissal application 23 days after the 21-day statutory period expired. The Commission refused an extension because he had no satisfactory explanation for the delay, knew of the dismissal immediately, and the remaining factors were neutral or only marginally supportive. The application was dismissed.

Key holding: In weighing the s 394(3) factors, a marginal favour from the applicant’s efforts to dispute dismissal is outweighed by the lack of a satisfactory reason for delay and immediate awareness of dismissal, so no exceptional circumstances are established.

Balancing the factor that weighs marginally in favour of a finding of exceptional circumstances, being the Applicant's efforts to dispute his dismissal, against the factors weighing more heavily against such a finding, being the lack of a satisfactory reason for delay and the Applicant's awareness of the dismissal on the day it was conveyed by the Respondent, I find that there are no exceptional circumstances in this matter.

entry.content:
Ms King applied under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for an unfair dismissal remedy after AMIT made her part-time finance/administrative role redundant in March 2026. The Commission had to decide whether the dismissal was a genuine redundancy under s 389, so that it was not unfair under s 385.

Key holding: A dismissal is a genuine redundancy only if all three limbs of s 389 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) are established: operational change removing the need for the job, consultation compliance, and no reasonable redeployment.

All three limbs of s 389 must be established for a dismissal to be a genuine redundancy.

entry.title: Mr David Peter Grant v Metric PCM [2026] FWC 3937
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission considered whether David Grant’s dismissal by Metric PCM Pty Ltd was a genuine redundancy after the EDL Energy contract ended. It found all three elements of genuine redundancy under s 389 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) were satisfied, notwithstanding informal consultation and temporary alternative duties. Metric PCM’s jurisdictional objection was upheld and Mr Grant’s unfair dismissal application was dismissed.

Key holding: A dismissal meeting the s 389 definition of genuine redundancy cannot be an unfair dismissal because the person cannot satisfy the definition in s 385.

Given my three findings above, Mr Grant's dismissal was a case of "genuine redundancy" as defined in s.389 of the FW Act. That means Mr Grant cannot satisfy the definition of an unfair dismissal in s.385 of the FW Act.

entry.title: Barresi v Cross Yarra Partnerships [2026] VSC 666
entry.content:
The plaintiff sought judicial review of a second Wrongs Act Medical Panel determination that his whole person impairment did not meet the threshold, after an earlier panel had found that it did. The Court followed Citywide Service Solutions Pty Ltd v Rosata in permitting the later panel to determine the same medical question, and rejected the challenge based on s 28LZG(4). The catchwords record “Appeal dismissed”.

Key holding: An asserted misunderstanding by a Medical Panel of s 28LZG(4) will not constitute jurisdictional error unless the misunderstanding was material to the determination, in the sense that the decision could realistically have been different.

Consequently, in my opinion, the plaintiff has not established that the asserted misunderstanding by the second Panel of s 28LZG(4) was material to the decision that the second Panel made and therefore jurisdictional error has not been established.

entry.title: Latif and Commissioner of the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2342
entry.content:
The Tribunal refused the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission’s application to dismiss Mr Latif’s review applications concerning deemed internal review decisions to affirm a permanent ban and registration renewal refusal for Horizon Solsolutions Australia Pty Ltd. The case concerned whether the Tribunal had jurisdiction, whether Mr Latif was “directly affected”, and whether deemed decisions arose under the ART Act. The dismissal application was dismissed, so the substantive review applications remain on foot.

Key holding: A decision-maker cannot isolate a separate non-reviewable “standing” decision from the NDIS Act s 100 internal review process; standing is a threshold matter within that process and may be assessed by the Tribunal in determining jurisdiction.

It is my characterisation that the issue of standing is inherently a threshold matter that should be addressed as an integral part of the internal review process under s 100 of the NDIS Act, rather than as a distinct and, in this case as submitted by the Respondent, a non-reviewable decision made under s 100(2) of that Act.

entry.title: GWN25 by his Litigation Representative the Public Advocate v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1535
entry.content:
GWN25 sought judicial review of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his visa under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Minister conceded jurisdictional error in light of Minister for Immigration and Citizenship v DVRL, and the parties jointly proposed certiorari and mandamus. The Federal Court set aside the Tribunal decision and remitted the matter for redetermination, with costs.

Key holding: When assessing community risk under the relevant ministerial direction, the Tribunal must consider the different levels of risk depending on the visa status the applicant would hold, where that issue is advanced and supported by evidence.

The effect of the full court's ruling in DVRL is that the Tribunal was obliged, when considering "... the risk to the Australian community ..." for the purposes of cl 8.1(2) of the applicable ministerial direction, to consider not merely the risk that the applicant might pose if his permanent visa were restored but also the risk that he might pose as the holder of an ongoing bridging visa.

entry.content:
In Vlasios Rotziokos v Futuresleep Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4040, the Fair Work Commission considered an unfair dismissal application by a casual production worker dismissed after removing his safety vest and singlet on the factory floor during a meal break. The Commission found there was a valid reason for dismissal and a fair process, and that inconsistent enforcement of a related PPE colour requirement did not outweigh those matters. The application was dismissed.

Key holding: A dismissal for a clear safety-policy breach is not unfair where there is a valid reason, procedural fairness and prior specific warnings, even if the employer inconsistently enforced a related aspect of the policy, provided that inconsistency is outweighed by the other s 387 matters.

It follows from the above that having considered each of the matters specified in s.387 of the Act, I am satisfied that the dismissal of the Applicant was not harsh, unjust, or unreasonable. That is because there was a valid reason for the dismissal , the process followed by the Respondent was procedurally fair, the Applicant had been previously warned in relation to the specific conduct, all of which outweighs the inconsistent application of the Procedure I have identified.

entry.title: Mr Taryq Mousley v Coles Supermarkets Australia Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 3854
entry.content:
Mr Mousley applied under s.365 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) alleging Coles took adverse action by reducing his shifts and terminating him because of a workers’ compensation claim and injury. Coles said the dismissal took effect on 13 May 2026, making the 10 June 2026 application seven days late. The Fair Work Commission granted an extension of time, finding exceptional circumstances because Mr Mousley did not receive the termination letter and Mr Angelo failed to clarify his employment status after reasonable inquiries.

Key holding: Exceptional circumstances under s.366(2) may be established by a combination of the employee not receiving the termination letter, reasonably inquiring about dismissal status, and the employer failing to clarify the dismissal.

Having regard to all of the matters listed at s.366(2) of the FW Act, I am satisfied that there are exceptional circumstances. The combination of Mr Mousley not receiving a termination letter from Coles, seeking to clarify his employment status with Mr Angelo on 15 and 17 May 2026 and not receiving a proper response from Mr Angelo are matters which in my view are out of the ordinary course, unusual, special or uncommon.

entry.title: Mr Ben Duscher v The Trustee For The Jetwave Marine Services Unit Trust [2026] FWC 3963
entry.content:
Ben Duscher brought an unfair dismissal application under s.394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) after his employment with Jetwave Marine Services Unit Trust ended when its Port Hedland operations closed. The Respondent objected on jurisdictional grounds that the dismissal was a genuine redundancy, and Deputy President O’Keeffe upheld that objection and dismissed the application.

Key holding: Whether it is reasonable to redeploy a redundant permanent employee into casual or restructured work requires a case-by-case assessment, including the casual employees’ unfair dismissal protection and whether the redundancy can be directly allocated to their casual positions.

While I am not rejecting outright the Applicant's take on Helensburg, I think that it would be very much a case-by-case assessment as to whether it was reasonable to dispense with casuals to create permanent roles in a redundancy scenario. It is fair to say that one of the elements might be the level of unfair dismissal protection the casuals have and whether the redundancy situation can be allocated directly to their casual positions.

entry.content:
The plaintiff sought judicial review of decisions revoking his Category AB firearms licence, including the original revocation and an internal review affirming it. The Supreme Court held only the internal review decision was operative and reviewable, found no failure to consider mandatory considerations or legal unreasonableness, and dismissed the summons.

Key holding: Where an original administrative decision is affirmed on internal review under s 53 of the ADR Act 1997 (NSW), only the review decision is legally operative and amenable to judicial review.

That conclusion, which was essentially argued by the defendant, means that, in the present circumstances, the second is the operative decision. It is only that decision which is amenable to judicial review.

entry.title: Younes v Younes (No 2) [2026] NSWSC 1261
entry.content:
Lolita Younes sought declaratory relief and specific performance concerning agreements relating to the subdivision/sale of the front block at 36 Page Street, Wentworthville. The substantive claim and Susie Younes’s cross-claim were dismissed by consent after subdivision and transfer to Lolita were completed. Stern J determined the reserved costs issue on the papers and made no order as to costs.

Key holding: Where proceedings are dismissed by consent without a merits determination, the court may make no order as to costs if it cannot conclude any party acted unreasonably or would have succeeded on the merits.

In these circumstances I am not satisfied that any one party has acted unreasonably in commencing or defending proceedings or that any one party would have been successful had the various claims been determined on their merits. Having regard to this, the appropriate order is that there be no order as to the costs of the proceedings
